criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household drinking-water service access, specifically municipal tap-water coverage within residential premises across Indian cities and towns.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes -> plain_criterion2_decision='include') because it empirically models administrative categories of urban local governments (municipal corporations, municipalities, town panchayats), per-capita intergovernmental infrastructure grant allocations (NURM/UIDSSMT), and a state-level fiscal decentralization index. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no -> decision='exclude', E03) because administrative categories and city size are used solely as proxies for general municipal resource/technical capacity, alongside macro fiscal decentralization and infrastructure grant funding, rather than any rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing access; indeed the paper explicitly notes it lacks data on city-level institutional configurations for water service delivery).
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical analysis using Census of India 2001 and 2011 data and state/municipal administrative statistics across 3,547 statutory cities and towns nested in 21 states.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports percentage-point change (improvement/growth) between 2001 and 2011 in the proportion of urban households whose primary water source is municipal tap water accessed within the residence.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis and population (3,547 statutory cities and towns in 21 Indian states), exposures (city size class, local government administrative category, per-capita intergovernmental grant aid, state fiscal decentralization and income), outcome (2001-2011 percentage-point change in in-dwelling tap-water coverage), and study design (multilevel linear regression with state random effects) are clearly identified, though the exposures do not meet the narrow Criterion 2 scope.

evidence_quotes.quote: urban households whose primary water source was tap water accessed within the residence, between the years 2001 and 2011.

I use administratively defined urban local government categories as a measure for local capacity. Urban local governments in India are categorized as municipal corporations, municipalities, or town councils (or panchayats) for administrative purposes.
I measure the impact of intergovernmental aid by including the amount of funds allocated towards water projects per capita for each city
This study is currently limited by the lack of data on institutional configurations for water service delivery at the city level

Since the data are grouped at the state-level and multilevel factors affect city-level outcomes, I use a nested multilevel linear regression model with random effects to account for both city-level and state-level variance.

raw_response.exposure: City size category (proxy for tax base), urban local government administrative category (municipal corporation, municipality, town panchayat as proxy for local government capacity), per-capita intergovernmental infrastructure grant aid (NURM/UIDSSMT), and state-level fiscal decentralization index, urbanization, and per-capita state income
raw_response.outcome: Percentage-point change (growth/improvement) between 2001 and 2011 in the city-level proportion of urban households whose primary water source was tap water accessed within the residence
raw_response.population_and_sample: 3,547 statutory cities and towns (urban local governments) nested within 21 states in India, enumerated in both the 2001 and 2011 Census of India
raw_response.rationale: This quantitative multilevel study examines 2001-2011 changes in household in-premise municipal tap-water coverage across 3,547 Indian cities and towns (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, c6). Under the broad/plain wording of Criterion 2 it would be included because it models local government administrative categories, intergovernmental grant transfers (NURM/UIDSSMT), and state fiscal decentralization. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): administrative categories and city size serve as macro proxies for municipal fiscal/technical capacity alongside intergovernmental infrastructure project funding and macro fiscal decentralization, without examining any rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (and the author explicitly notes the absence of data on city-level institutional configurations for water service delivery).
raw_response.study_design: Quantitative observational multilevel linear regression (state random-effects model of 2001-2011 city-level panel change)
